Abstract:

Sustainable development requires not only sustained economic growth but also the accumulation and equitable distribution of productive assets that support long-term well-being. In this context, comprehensive wealth, incorporating produced capital, human capital, natural capital, and net foreign assets, provides a broader measure of sustainability. Despite its growing importance, comprehensive wealth remains unevenly distributed across developing countries, raising concerns regarding convergence, distributional inequalities and the sustainability of their productive asset base. Against this background, this study aims to examine the dynamics and determinants of comprehensive wealth in developing countries as delineated in the following objectives. First, to investigate the convergence or divergence patterns of comprehensive wealth. Second, to assess inequality-adjusted comprehensive wealth and the role of socio-economic and demographic factors, including institutional quality and financial inclusion, in explaining its distribution. Third, to study the role of structural transformation and technological innovation in influencing comprehensive wealth. Lastly, to analyse comprehensive wealth-based total factor productivity across developing countries. It further examines productivity changes and their decomposition. The study employs secondary panel data from various sources, including the World Bank's Wealth Account, World Development Indicators, Worldwide Governance Indicators, and other international databases, covering 2000 to 2023 for developing countries. Appropriate econometric techniques will be used for the empirical analysis. The study seeks to provide a multifaceted understanding of comprehensive wealth and generate policy insights to strengthen the productive asset base and promote inclusive and sustainable development in developing countries.
